strengths: Clinically well-motivated approach: the region-focused design emulates the actual radiologist workflow (global overview followed by organ-based analysis), and structured per-region report generation is a sensible direction for 3D CT reporting.

The R² Token Pooling provides a practical and efficient tokenization scheme for 3D CT (D + T tokens instead of D × T), addressing a real computational bottleneck in slice-wise 3D MLLMs, and the region-centric slow-token selection is a reasonable improvement over uniform sampling (supported by the LITA ablation).

Comprehensive evaluation protocol combining NLG metrics (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, METEOR), clinical metrics (CA-F1 via RadBERT, GREEN), and LLM-as-judge scoring; ablations isolate the contribution of each component and show consistent gains from the full model.
Fair comparison protocol: all baselines use the same LLM decoder (LLaMA3-8B), same input resolution, and identical compute/time budgets, which strengthens the credibility of the benchmark.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: implementation details (LoRA settings, training schedule, hardware) are provided, pseudo-mask generation via SAT is specified, and the authors state the code will be publicly released.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework is largely an assembly of existing components — R² pooling is LITA's slow/fast token scheme with a region-centric slice selection heuristic; the Mask-Driven Visual Extractor is adopted from MAIRA-SEG/Osprey with minimal 3D adaptation; pseudo-masks come from SAT; and Patient-Specific Attributes follow RadGPT/Insight. The main contribution is the integration, which is valuable but incremental.

Quantitative gains are modest and inconsistent: BLEU-4 improves marginally over M3D (0.290 vs. 0.288), while ROUGE-L (0.375 vs. 0.391) and METEOR (0.494 vs. 0.497) are actually worse than M3D. Only CA-F1 and GPT-4 score improve, and no statistical significance testing or variance across runs is reported.

A closely related baseline is missing: Reg2RG [52], which also uses universal segmentation models to extract organ pseudo-masks combined with global features for CT report generation, is directly comparable and should have been benchmarked. Its absence weakens the claim of state-of-the-art performance.

The evaluation setup introduces potential circularity: ground-truth reports are constructed by reassigning grounded sentences to six regions using the same segmentation-derived region definitions that also drive the Patient-Specific Attribute extractor and region-token selection. The structured region-split format is not validated clinically and may bias NLG metrics in favor of the proposed method's output format.

Qualitative evidence is thin: only a single COVID-19 case is shown. Additional diverse examples (and ideally a reader study or clinician assessment) would be needed to substantiate claims of superior clinical utility and interpretability.

Some claims lack support: the explanation that CT2Rep's higher GREEN score is 'biased due to overfitting to normal cases' is speculative and unverified; GPT-4o Mini as evaluator has questionable reliability for nuanced medical factuality judgments; and there is a table caption error ('MS-VLM') and minor typos ('legion' for 'lesion', 'Extention') that suggest insufficient polish.

No discussion of limitations or societal impact despite the medical application: risks of propagating segmentation-model errors (SAT pseudo-masks) into reports, hallucination from text-attribute prompts, and the safety implications of automated radiology reporting are not addressed.

strengths: The paper is clinically well-motivated: emulating the radiologist workflow (global overview followed by region-by-region analysis) is a sensible framing for 3D CT report generation, and the structured 6-region report format is a reasonable design choice.

The token-efficiency problem in 3D medical MLLMs is real, and the R² Token Pooling idea (dense global tokens + sparse region-representative slow tokens selected by pseudo-mask coverage) is a simple, sensible adaptation of the slow-fast token paradigm from video to CT.
The evaluation covers multiple complementary metric families (NLG metrics, RadBERT-based CA-F1, GREEN, LLM-as-judge), which is more comprehensive than many report-generation papers.
Ablation variants isolate each proposed component (R², Mask, Attr), and the comparison protocol controls compute (48-hour, 2×A100 budget, shared LLaMA3-8B decoder), which is a fair-minded setup.
The supplementary material provides training details, implementation specifics, and the deterministic attribute-extraction pseudocode, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. All three claimed contributions are direct adaptations of existing techniques: R² Token Pooling is LITA's slow-fast tokens with a different slice-selection rule; the Mask-Driven Visual Extractor explicitly reuses MAIRA-SEG's/Osprey's mask-aware extractor with the same hyperparameters; and Patient-Specific Attributes reuses the RadGPT/Insight deterministic vision-translator idea. The paper is essentially an assembly of these components applied to RadGenome-Chest CT, and the paper itself acknowledges this lineage.

Marginal and inconsistent quantitative gains. Full-model improvements over the strongest baseline (M3D) are within noise (BLEU-4 0.290 vs 0.288; ROUGE-L is worse, 0.375 vs 0.391; METEOR is worse, 0.494 vs 0.497). No statistical significance testing is reported. The ablation table itself shows Ablation-R²+Attr beating the full model on BLEU-4 (0.293 vs 0.290), and the GREEN score is substantially worse than CT2Rep (0.278 vs 0.374) — dismissed in a single sentence as a 'biased result' of overfitting to normal cases without any supporting analysis. Selective narrative around mixed results weakens the SOTA claim.

Potential information leakage that could inflate the headline metric. The paper feeds Patient-Specific Attributes (lesion counts, diameters, locations) extracted from pseudo-masks directly into the LLM as text prompts. On RadGenome-Chest CT, masks are grounded to report sentences — lesion masks may literally encode findings stated in the reference report. Injecting derived lesion statistics as prompts risks leaking ground-truth content into the generator, which could explain the CA-F1 and GPT-4 gains. The paper does not discuss whether lesion masks come from the dataset's grounded annotations or from independently run SAT inference, nor does it ablate this confound.

The GPT-4 score relies on GPT-4o Mini as judge with prompts from M3D; LLM-as-judge scores are noisy and prompt-sensitive, and no human expert evaluation is provided despite the paper's clinical claims.

Single dataset, single domain (chest CT), low input resolution (256×256×32), and no external validation. Generalization claims (e.g., extension to other modalities/regions in the conclusion) are unsupported.

Clarity and polish issues undermine confidence: Table 1's caption refers to 'MS-VLM' (a method name that never appears elsewhere in the paper), suggesting copy-paste; the 'Ours' row is inconsistently labeled as 'Ablation-R²+Attr+Mask'; there are typos ('Extention', 'Quantitive', 'legion' for 'lesion' in the pseudocode); and the exact source of lesion pseudo-masks (SAT inference vs. dataset-provided grounded masks) is left ambiguous.

The claim that 'the code for our framework is publicly available' is not verifiable from the manuscript (no URL provided), and given the paper's heavy dependence on component re-implementation details, reproducibility claims need substantiation.

The motivation for region-focused generation is undercut by the evaluation: reports are evaluated as merged full reports, and the paper provides no region-level analysis demonstrating that region tokens/mask tokens actually improve per-region accuracy as claimed.

strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem: region-specific interpretation for 3D chest CT report generation, motivated by a realistic radiologist workflow (global overview followed by region-focused analysis and clinical integration).

The framework is well-organized into three components (R2 Token Pooling, Mask-Driven Visual Extractor, Patient-Specific Attribute Extractor), and each component is clearly described with implementation details (LLaMA3-8B, Rad-DINO, LoRA settings, token counts) provided in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.

Evaluation uses a multi-faceted metric suite (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, METEOR, CA-F1, GREEN, and an LLM-based GPT-4 score), and the paper includes both quantitative comparisons to four open-source 3D baselines and component-wise ablations (R2, +Mask, +Attr, and LITA-style uniform sampling).

The structured, region-split report generation scheme with six anatomical regions is a reasonable and interpretable design choice, and the qualitative example (Fig. 3) illustrates that component removal leads to clinically visible failures (e.g., Ablation-R2 missing ground-glass opacities).
The paper is generally well written and positions its contributions against a thorough body of related work spanning medical MLLMs, 3D vision encoders, region-focused MLLMs, and prompt-based methods.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework is largely a 3D adaptation of existing components—MAIRA-SEG's mask-aware extractor (built on Osprey), LITA's slow/fast token scheme, SAT pseudo-masks, and RadGPT-style deterministic attribute extraction. The primary novelty is the region-centric slow-token sampling (selecting slices by pseudo-mask pixel count) and the 3D restructuring, which is a relatively incremental modification.

The claimed 'state-of-the-art' performance is weakly supported: gains over the strongest baseline (M3D) are marginal or negative on several metrics (BLEU-4 0.290 vs 0.288; ROUGE-L 0.375 vs 0.391; METEOR 0.494 vs 0.497; GREEN 0.278 vs 0.297), with meaningful improvements only on CA-F1 (0.450 vs 0.435) and the GPT-4 score. No statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported for any comparison.

Potential evaluation leakage: the ground-truth training text is constructed by splitting reports according to the same six pseudo-mask-defined regions, and the Patient-Specific Attributes are derived from the very same SAT pseudo-masks used to define the region structure and ground-truth sentence allocation. Quantitative attributes (volumes, lesion counts, diameters) fed as text prompts may partially encode ground-truth content, inflating CA-F1 and LLM-evaluator scores relative to baselines that receive no such metadata. This confound is not discussed or ablated (e.g., no baseline-plus-attributes comparison).

The GPT-4o Mini evaluator, with prompts borrowed from M3D, is a noisy and somewhat dated choice; no human expert evaluation or radiologist study is provided, which is especially important for claims of 'clinical relevance' and 'interpretability'.

Qualitative analysis rests on a single case (COVID-19 pneumonia). Broader or representative qualitative examples, failure cases, and analysis of the six-region merging step are missing. The claim of 'interpretability' is asserted but not empirically demonstrated (e.g., no region-level fidelity evaluation).

Baseline fairness is questionable: baselines were constrained to 48 hours on two A100 GPUs and 'trained from scratch or fine-tuned' under a common setup, but the paper's own text attributes CT2Rep's weak performance to insufficient training resources—suggesting baselines may be under-trained. A table caption also references 'MS-VLM', which does not correspond to any method in the paper, indicating insufficient care in preparation.

Ablation results contain unexplained anomalies: Ablation-R2+Mask achieves the best METEOR (0.498) yet a sharply lower GPT-4 score (44.457 vs 48.837 for the full model), and Ablation-R2+Attr achieves higher BLEU-4 (0.293) than the full model; the paper offers only speculative interpretations, and the labeling in Table 1 ('Ours (Ablation-R2+Attr+Mask)') is confusing.

Comparison setup may disadvantage full-report baselines: the proposed model generates region-wise reports merged into a final report against region-split ground truth, while baselines presumably generate full reports; how this format difference affects NLG metrics is not analyzed.

There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion, which is a notable omission for a clinical AI paper. Minor issues (e.g., 'Extention', 'legion' for 'lesion' in the pseudocode) further suggest the manuscript needed another polish pass.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated, clinically grounded framework (MedRegion-CT) that coherently combines three components—Region-based SlowFast Tokenizer, Mask-Driven Visual Extractor, and Lesion Attribute Extractor—to shift 3D CT report generation from global to region-aware representations, mirroring the radiology workflow.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons against five recent 3D medical MLLMs on both an internal (RadGenome-Chest CT) and an external cross-institutional benchmark with 95% CIs, a component ablation including external encoder baselines (M3Denc., LITAenc.), size-stratified nodule analysis, a blinded radiologist reader study showing a large margin (6.98 vs. 4.44), and a segmentation-noise stress test (Tab. S5) that honestly probes the framework's dependence on pseudo-mask quality.

The new Structured Chest CT Report Generation Benchmark, with a documented multi-stage NLP pipeline for converting unstructured reports into six clinically relevant sections, is a useful community resource and supports both in-domain and zero-shot cross-institutional evaluation.

Limitations are disclosed candidly (e.g., degraded detection of small nodules ≤5mm³ traced to TotalSegmentator false negatives, weaker airway performance, dependence on upstream segmentation quality), and the code is stated to be publicly available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integrative rather than fundamental: the SlowFast tokenizer adapts video-domain ideas (LITA/SlowFast-LLaVA), the mask-pooling extractor closely follows Osprey with volumetric pooling, pseudo-masks come from an off-the-shelf TotalSegmentator (as in Reg2RG/MAIRA-SEG), and structured textual lesion attributes echo prior prompt-based approaches (e.g., RadGPT, PromptMRG). The paper does not compare against the closest region-guided CT methods (Reg2RG, MAIRA-SEG-style segmentation-aware pipelines), making it hard to isolate the contribution over prior mask-guided report generation.

Benchmark validity is a significant concern: both training labels and evaluation references are produced by an LLM-based restructuring pipeline (DSPy + Llama-3.3-70B) whose output quality is never human-validated, and the headline 'Clinical Accuracy' metric is computed by GPT-5-nano against these same LLM-refined references. This circularity could inflate apparent clinical gains; a manual audit of the structured labels and a sensitivity analysis of the LLM-judge are needed.

The framework inherits a hard floor from the upstream segmentor: on small nodules the detection rate (0.1270) is roughly half that of the baselines (0.29-0.37, Tab. S3), meaning the method can be substantially worse for clinically important micro-lesions; only 110/160 cases were analyzed and no mitigation (e.g., a dedicated detector ensemble) is explored.

Several details undermine precision of the method description: the Slow Pathway equation (Eq. 3, subsampling m(i,2j)) is ambiguously specified; the ablation is run on only a 30% training subset; and the reader study involves a single reader on 50 cases, limiting statistical strength. Some external-dataset confidence intervals overlap substantially across variants (e.g., GREEN in Tab. 2), weakening claims of consistent superiority in zero-shot transfer.

Radiation of scope/clinical risk is not discussed: no error-analysis taxonomy of hallucination severity, no discussion of how quantitative attribute errors (from the deterministic extractor) could propagate into confidently wrong reports—important for a clinical-facing system, though IRB approval is documented for the external data.

strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem: region-aware 3D CT report generation. The core idea of using pseudo-masks from a universal segmentation model to guide both tokenization (Region-based SlowFast Tokenizer) and token extraction (Mask-Driven Visual Extractor) is a sensible adaptation of known techniques (SlowFast [11], Osprey [48]) to the 3D medical domain.

The Lesion Attribute Extractor is a practical contribution: encoding deterministic, quantitative lesion measurements (volume, diameter, location) as textual prompts provides verifiable clinical evidence to the LLM, reducing hallucination risk in a way that is transparent and reproducible.

The experimental evidence is fairly comprehensive: comparisons against five recent 3D medical MLLMs on both an internal benchmark and a cross-institutional external set (zero-shot), an ablation study of all three components, a size-stratified nodule analysis, a radiologist reader study, and a segmentation-noise stress test. 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap are reported.
The structured chest CT report benchmark, with a documented multi-stage NLP pipeline for report restructuring, is a potentially useful community resource, and code is stated to be publicly available.

Limitations are discussed candidly (e.g., small-nodule sensitivity bounded by upstream TotalSegmentator false negatives, airway feature dilution, mask-quality dependence), which strengthens the paper's scientific credibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: each component is largely a recombination of existing methods (SlowFast dual-rate tokenization from video LLMs, Osprey-style mask pooling, TotalSegmentator pseudo-masks, text-prompting of clinical attributes). The paper is best viewed as a well-engineered applied/systems contribution rather than a fundamentally new algorithm, and the framing in the introduction somewhat overstates the novelty.

The ground-truth structured reports are themselves produced by an LLM-based pipeline (Llama-3.3-70B with DSPy), and clinical metrics (GPT-CA) use gpt-5-nano. Evaluating model output against LLM-restructured references and scoring with an LLM judge introduces potential circularity and bias; no human validation of the report-restructuring pipeline's fidelity is provided beyond a limited reader study.

The reader study is weak: a single reader (a senior resident, not an attending radiologist) scoring only 50 cases on a subjective 1-10 scale. This limits the strength of the claim of 'clinical accuracy' and 'minimized hallucinations.'

Small-nodule detection is substantially worse than several baselines (0.127 vs. 0.365 for CT-CHAT in Tab. S3), meaning the region-prioritized design inherits the biases of the upstream segmenter. The model's gains are therefore contingent on segmentation quality, as the authors' own stress test (Tab. S5) confirms a large BLEU drop (0.3273 -> 0.2252) with distorted organ masks.

The ablation is conducted on only a 30% training subset, and some absolute external scores are low (GREEN 0.1572, GPT-CA 0.2642), so the zero-shot generalization claims should be interpreted cautiously.

Presentation issues: the external dataset and some dataset references appear as blank/redacted names throughout (e.g., 'the external [blank] dataset'), which hinders reproducibility and clarity even under anonymization; Eq. (1) is essentially a definition rather than a technical contribution; Eq. (2)/(3) notation (AvgPool with kernel=T over variable-length slice sets) is under-specified.

Several key details that affect reproducibility (token counts per pathway, hyperparameters of the NLP report-restructuring pipeline, prompt templates for the LLM metrics) are deferred to the supplement or unclear in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and clearly motivated problem: shifting from global volumetric representations to region-aware 3D encoding for CT report generation. The analogy to the radiologist's coarse-to-fine workflow is well articulated and consistently used to justify each design choice.

The technical framework is coherent and well-organized. The Region-based SlowFast Tokenizer (mask-guided fast/slow pathways, Eqs. 2-3), the Mask-Driven Visual Extractor (multi-layer volumetric mask pooling, Eqs. 4-5), and the deterministic Lesion Attribute Extractor (Eqs. 6-7, Supplementary Algorithm 1) are each clearly described and reproducible.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: in-domain results on RadGenome-Chest CT plus a zero-shot external multi-institutional benchmark, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all numbers, region-wise analysis (Tab. S1), size-stratified nodule analysis (Tab. S3), a blinded radiologist reader study (Tab. S4), a mask-perturbation robustness stress test (Tab. S5), a component-wise ablation against alternative encoder baselines (Tab. 2), and qualitative comparisons (Fig. 3, Fig. S1).

The construction of a structured, six-region chest CT report benchmark from RadGenome-Chest CT via a documented multi-stage NLP pipeline (DSPy + Llama-3.3-70B) is a useful community contribution, and the code/data release commitment supports reproducibility.

The ablation convincingly isolates the contribution of each module, and the external-dataset ablation demonstrates that the gains (particularly from the attribute prompts and the regional tokenizer over M3D/LITA encoders) transfer across institutions rather than being an artifact of in-domain fitting.

The limitations that do exist (e.g., failure on very small nodules due to TotalSegmentator false negatives, weaker performance on the large airway) are honestly identified and analyzed, which strengthens rather than undermines the scientific case.
weaknesses: The individual technical components are largely adaptations of existing ideas: the SlowFast strategy from video recognition [11,19,46], mask pooling from Osprey [48], pseudo-mask-driven region tokens as in MAIRA-SEG [37] and Reg2RG [7], and attribute-as-text prompting [22,47]. The contribution is a well-executed integration for 3D chest CT rather than a fundamentally new technique, which reviewers at a general vision venue may view as incremental.

There is a potential information-leakage concern with the Lesion Attribute Extractor: since lesion prompts are deterministically computed from segmentation masks, part of the reported improvement (especially in clinical metrics) may reflect the model copying structured numeric prompts into the report rather than genuine visual understanding. A control experiment feeding randomized or deliberately wrong attribute values at inference (not just the coarse 'Distorted' mask setting in Tab. S5) would strengthen the claim.

Ground-truth reports for both training and evaluation are generated by an LLM-based restructuring pipeline rather than curated by clinicians; errors or stylistic biases introduced by Llama-3.3-70B could propagate into all reported metrics, and the paper does not report any quality audit (e.g., human verification rate) of the restructured reports. The reader study (50 cases, single reader) partially mitigates this but is small.

Reliance on LM-as-judge metrics (GREEN, CRG, GPT-CA with the gpt-5-nano API) introduces uncertainty about judge reliability and possible bias toward the structured output style the proposed model is trained to produce; combined with the structured prompt design, some advantage on LM-based metrics may be format-driven. The divergence between NLG and clinical metrics on the external set is acknowledged but not fully disentangled.

The ablation study uses only a 30% training subset, while the main comparison uses the full dataset; it is not guaranteed that component contributions hold at full scale. Also, the small-nodule detection rate for the proposed method (0.1270 in Tab. S3) is substantially worse than all baselines (0.28-0.36), and the attribution of this to the upstream segmentor, while plausible, is not verified against, e.g., an ensemble or alternative segmentor.

Some clarity issues remain: Eq. 2's notation (AvgPool with kernel=T over a per-slice token set, combined with a mask condition outside the set) is confusing; the external dataset name is redacted in several places leaving its provenance only partially characterizable; and the choice of GPT-5-nano (rather than a stronger judge) for clinical accuracy is not justified.

The framework is tightly coupled to a chest-CT-specific six-region taxonomy aligned with TotalSegmentator's label space; the claimed modularity is asserted but not demonstrated empirically on another anatomical domain or with a different segmentor.
